A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -6 & -3 \\ 2 & 5 & 6 \\ 1 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ which of the following could be the matrix $P?$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ is a diagonalization of the matrix $A.$ So let's apply the diagonalization algorithm to $A.$

**Step 1.** From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-7\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=7.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- Consider $\lambda =-7.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -6 & -3 \\ 2 & 5 & 6 \\ 1 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-7)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 & -3 \\ 2 & 12 & 6 \\ 1 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & 12 & 6 & 0 \\ 1 & 6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

As a result, we have two linearly independent eigenvectors

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- Consider $\lambda =7.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -6 & -3 \\ 2 & 5 & 6 \\ 1 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-15 & -6 & -3 \\ 2 & -2 & 6 \\ 1 & 6 & -11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking for nonzero solutions of $(A-7I)x=0,$ we obtain the eigenvector 

$\,$ ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the invertible matrix $P$ using our eigenvectors, as follows:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "debc197f-086e-55eb-b1ea-1023d09ebd2f"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "290c2d0a-3e1a-5fa6-bb40-54236727b6e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-4A+I) & =O \\ A-4I+{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =4I-A\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(6-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )+33 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{13}$ | $+$ | $x$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-3\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{15}$ | $\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$ |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,5x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,+$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$ |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,3x$ |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,2x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,+$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\  & =-2A+6I \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124552 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124361 :question/id #uuid "95b44b17-b796-51eb-93dd-4ee4b2e5c3f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5894"} :knowledge-point/id $$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

$$
\det(A-\lambda I),
$$

For instance, let's find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix ![](images/1d/1d6d0bdedbb25bbc41759e443cdc0f6a207ef5cbfa4761b05e1a1a2eda24cbec.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(C-\lambda I) \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| \\  & =(-8-\lambda )\cdot (7-\lambda )-(-9)\cdot 6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25396b96-19ec-592d-b1c4-3c6fa172ef08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3580 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9083e01a-4e57-589b-9b08-48ecc4af0075" :step/math-academy-id 20133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125433}} {:db/id 17592186125430 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following: 

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.
$$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](images/d2/d24f480293267a9ddc28b03626e7bde6f01bd62a136fed17f8580bf1ea34d776.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,
$$

we have

$$
p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86101838-75af-5a3f-9dae-1e63a94c77a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3581 :tutorial/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "7b3b4f95-8159-5533-bd80-db194716f75b" :tutorial/content "What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/8e/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} :step/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 21546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125430}} {:db/id 17592186125502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "4e500723-739c-51c7-b82e-8727a24a1b1f" :step/math-academy-id 20137 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125455}} {:db/id 17592186125430 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following: 

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.
$$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](images/d2/d24f480293267a9ddc28b03626e7bde6f01bd62a136fed17f8580bf1ea34d776.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,
$$

we have

$$
p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86101838-75af-5a3f-9dae-1e63a94c77a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3581 :tutorial/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "7b3b4f95-8159-5533-bd80-db194716f75b" :step/math-academy-id 20134 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125432}} {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following:

For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this." :tutorial/id #uuid "769ceb10-1667-52b6-8a89-b4c7ca835276" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4448 :tutorial/title "Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "3167e19f-42e7-5fc7-8ee9-fb73a5fa3da3" :step/math-academy-id 27370 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125434}} {:db/id 17592186125796 :tutorial/content "What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/8e/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} {:db/id 17592186125455 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124552 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124361 :question/id #uuid "95b44b17-b796-51eb-93dd-4ee4b2e5c3f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5894"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "87febdb4-5f54-5aff-b84a-1b05359d6b57" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050376} {:db/id 17592186050669}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125139} {:db/id 17592186125141} {:db/id 17592186272119} {:db/id 17592186326707} {:db/id 17592186351499} {:db/id 17592186351500} {:db/id 17592186351501} {:db/id 17592186354441} {:db/id 17592186354442} {:db/id 17592186430411}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "f3faf291-dd20-56c9-bc3d-8482113b6764" :step/math-academy-id 21546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125430}} {:db/id 17592186125434 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124538 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124347 :question/id #uuid "ce724b3b-f440-5c1f-86a6-c50a54931233" :question/math-academy-id "e-5512"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "787173e1-f957-5ff0-9d14-a6ccb11de1d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050117}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125096} {:db/id 17592186125106} {:db/id 17592186272142} {:db/id 17592186272144} {:db/id 17592186323938} {:db/id 17592186323939} {:db/id 17592186326709} {:db/id 17592186354448} {:db/id 17592186354451} {:db/id 17592186392147} {:db/id 17592186392218} {:db/id 17592186392225}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "0fed3d43-139d-505f-8482-70f3be0516d6" :step/math-academy-id 20138} {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. $$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{8},$ $q=-\frac{1}{8}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{8}+(-\frac{1}{8})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "37974a8d-1c28-54c7-b296-b5b3c2e14d09" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440845}} {:db/id 17592186440843 :step/content {:db/id 17592186354443 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23996cc9-567a-51b9-98b0-2f94757720ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{A}^{2}-3A+16I" :db/id 17592186351889} {:answer/id #uuid "3b9440a6-7475-5119-a281-5c4281a46f22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{A}^{2}-3A+6I" :db/id 17592186352117} {:answer/id #uuid "a1e14de5-77a9-57b7-8420-3ce37cbf93ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3A-16I" :db/id 17592186352952} {:answer/id #uuid "b5a9477d-b279-5e07-bb55-bcddccdb5c4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{A}^{2}+3A-16I" :db/id 17592186353124} {:answer/id #uuid "dedacf6f-daed-557d-84e3-a6bbb9be9999" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3A+16I" :db/id 17592186353503}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186351889} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb1e7ca4-8013-510f-a476-bdfe0c462d57" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186354164}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "03d6fc6a-0f72-5d35-ba67-c4e4d25be4dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-85924" :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix with the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{3}-{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -16.$ Then, ${A}^{3}=$" :question/worked-solution "Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{3}-{A}^{2}+3A-16I & =O \\ {A}^{3} & ={A}^{2}-3A+16I.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "864708dc-01cf-5025-81a5-3d649155dedc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440842}} {:db/id 17592186440844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326708 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28cc5ee2-6da9-52c1-a92b-8edb26634139" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{6}" :db/id 17592186324300} {:answer/id #uuid "47e93b3f-33d7-5090-b1fc-02844e927bff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{6}" :db/id 17592186324553} {:answer/id #uuid "a44579f4-a9e4-53da-a506-9eefbb4bf2e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186325367} {:answer/id #uuid "bd8f6f17-d42e-553d-a74b-0e76268b5611" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186325601} {:answer/id #uuid "d1b95922-aad1-5b77-a0d0-e6a698ab713b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186325792}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324300} :answer-field/id #uuid "36035083-9336-58a8-9968-10256743cb12" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326311}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "688a2834-9fcd-5275-97a0-97e7aaa1b79c" :question/math-academy-id "q-38704" :question/problem "Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

:question/problem "Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{16}-4{x}^{14}+7x-3\,$, find $f(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">${x}^{16}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$4{x}^{14}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>

<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$7x$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$3$</td>

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\  & =7A-3I \\  & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$4^{8} \cdot \left(\dfrac{7}{4}\right)^5$ as the product of two exponentiated integers." :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the second factor using the power of quotient rule:

$$
4^{8} \cdot (\frac{7}{4})^{5} = 4^{8} \cdot \frac{7^{5}}{4^{5}}
$$

Next, we rewrite the fractional part of our expression as follows:

$$
4^{8} \cdot \dfrac{7^5}{4^5} = \dfrac{4^8}{4^5} \cdot 7^5
$$

Finally, we simplify using the quotient rule for exponents:

- **Quotient rule**: to divide powers of the same base, subtract the exponents.
- **Power rule**: to raise a power to another power, multiply the exponents.
- **Power of product rule**: to raise the product of two numbers to a power, raise each number to that power, and then multiply.
- **Power of quotient rule**: to raise a fraction to a power, raise both the numerator and the denominator to that power.

are given below. What is $[x]_{B}?$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}],\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot (-4)-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351438 :question/id #uuid "1a8774bf-f531-5684-a4ee-be071e1e5ed5" :question/math-academy-id "q-82599"} {:db/id 17592186351452 :question/id #uuid "48c0bf71-b661-5e47-9c9b-1a61e9513017" :question/math-academy-id "q-82705"} {:db/id 17592186386696 :question/id #uuid "6ed39867-0f3e-5f3d-ab65-536828c9ba67" :question/math-academy-id "q-113573" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ef569771-c4e7-5291-a02a-eccb98516f64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 42\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186386698} {:answer/id #uuid "19f40148-c027-5e57-83ca-f9ce5e2e487f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 13\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186386699} {:answer/id #uuid "f2dbac90-d79d-5e74-a3e8-3e28846fd99d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186386700} {:answer/id #uuid "8aadec7c-66e6-5275-836d-0b2d825fbd7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 18\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186386701} {:answer/id #uuid "54154bb7-e3f6-55f0-b690-aed92908791b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 26\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186386702}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186386701} :answer-field/id #uuid "30675a92-d5d0-5d0c-a77d-9c525c8b8db4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186386697}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ to $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is given below. $$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-8)-(-3)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-8 & 3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

:question/problem "$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 16\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 16-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186247377 :question/id #uuid "ca416b56-0c6d-5fb5-8b76-d2124cfd2e38" :question/math-academy-id "q-113600"} {:db/id 17592186247379 :question/id #uuid "162a4f62-2177-5623-998d-5746dbddde07" :question/math-academy-id "q-113606" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05662116-9ed5-51f3-a508-b1ed64f2e349" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186244359} {:answer/id #uuid "33a9596f-e4e0-5e92-b079-84b8cbdda157" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -11\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186244776} {:answer/id #uuid "7294001d-9a70-5e64-8833-bfc2b3f3c0db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}25 \\ 6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186245337} {:answer/id #uuid "b6b79f00-6365-55a2-9673-e57f0f1960c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 21\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186245947} {:answer/id #uuid "f5b08e24-4041-566d-9201-1f4cbd15de31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}19 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186246483}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186244359} :answer-field/id #uuid "12b31fac-75a2-50ec-9978-bbb512fe8ff1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186246582}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

"$$
B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given above. Find $[x]_{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & -6 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\},\,C=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186440463 :question/id #uuid "4f73a710-afa9-5a82-9ac8-46435d104af8" :question/math-academy-id "q-113707"} {:db/id 17592186440467 :question/id #uuid seen that to find the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to a basis $\mathcal B,$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B}.\end{aligned}
$$

In expanded form, the formula looks as follows:
![](images/89/890f34433211786e2cb8aa71057de40bdf3b12678c2bbb5a79ef5e680555937f.svg)

Also, remember that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}
	\quad\textrm{and}\quad
	P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cfffdf8e-9e9f-5304-8249-54a094cc7c11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4435 :tutorial/title "The Change-of-Basis Formula in Expanded Form"} :step/id #uuid "4c4259ae-ebd7-5d31-ae41-72156cefc066" :step/math-academy-id 27272 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125362}} {:db/id 17592186125667 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125708 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Now, suppose we would like to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ 

- We first need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 \mathbf{c}_1+x_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/58/58010a2a5206e3fc27e3d924de70cf32dcc92c3578bdb2821ace7278fbb223cf.svg)

- Similarly, we need to find $y_1$ and $y_2$ such that 

$$
y_1 \mathbf{c}_1+y_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/68/68788aa3e388c5cba14662a947c1b7afaacb95f611c256d11a7a6d7614c352b9.svg)

We can solve both systems using Gaussian elimination. However, we can do that simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](images/4b/4b00a4cbd7831f6da6acd06a087d5453bd455a89eb81f6b3036b1b572bb064d1.svg)

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get a matrix of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & {x}_{1} & {y}_{1} \\ 0 & 1 & {x}_{2} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where the required coefficients will be stored in the columns on the right-hand side." :tutorial/id #uuid "d42ee304-2e1f-5cc2-b334-65d083ea7323" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13287 :tutorial/title "Using Gaussian Elimination to Find the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis"} :step/id #uuid "184b8c31-de1a-5e34-ad87-2f626c830182" :step/math-academy-id 462199 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125498}}] :activity/title "Changing a Basis Using the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124710} {:db/id 17592186125361 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125768 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to $\mathcal B,$ we can use the **change-of-basis formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B},\end{aligned}
$$

where we recall that

- $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ respectively, and

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by
![](images/d9/d9388f46f84cc0c6b1d7e5cf43ee973085366ae4f44cfe74515c59bfc1994662.svg)

Let $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and ![](images/f9/f99f37621c20057077eb7c6e23690a45159cfe1b665c6b88b4a604f8687728bf.svg) Then we can easily find $[\,\mathbf{v}\,]_{\mathcal{C}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,v\,]_{C} & =\overset{{P}_{B\to C}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot \overset{[v]_{B}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "827e9581-9fde-5941-ad91-2c364796e5b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3217 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125500 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125822 :tutorial/content "We've seen that to find the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to a basis $\mathcal B,$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B}.\end{aligned}

In expanded form, the formula looks as follows:
![](images/89/890f34433211786e2cb8aa71057de40bdf3b12678c2bbb5a79ef5e680555937f.svg)

P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}

:step/content {:db/id 17592186125708 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Now, suppose we would like to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ 

- We first need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 \mathbf{c}_1+x_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/58/58010a2a5206e3fc27e3d924de70cf32dcc92c3578bdb2821ace7278fbb223cf.svg)

- Similarly, we need to find $y_1$ and $y_2$ such that 

$$
y_1 \mathbf{c}_1+y_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/68/68788aa3e388c5cba14662a947c1b7afaacb95f611c256d11a7a6d7614c352b9.svg)

We can solve both systems using Gaussian elimination. However, we can do that simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](images/4b/4b00a4cbd7831f6da6acd06a087d5453bd455a89eb81f6b3036b1b572bb064d1.svg)

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get a matrix of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & {x}_{1} & {y}_{1} \\ 0 & 1 & {x}_{2} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where the required coefficients will be stored in the columns on the right-hand side." :tutorial/id #uuid "d42ee304-2e1f-5cc2-b334-65d083ea7323" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13287 :tutorial/title "Using Gaussian Elimination to Find the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis"} :step/id #uuid "184b8c31-de1a-5e34-ad87-2f626c830182" :step/math-academy-id 462199 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125498}} {:db/id 17592186125498 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124577 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124384 :question/id #uuid "f04f55d3-40ec-52a8-a762-d8ac7090b8b8" :question/math-academy-id "e-7276"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "36f8f02f-acbd-5930-bd0c-8675ac868577" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048920}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124992} {:db/id 17592186125041} {:db/id 17592186247393} {:db/id 17592186247395} {:db/id 17592186351440} {:db/id 17592186351443} {:db/id 17592186351454} {:db/id 17592186386703} {:db/id 17592186394449} {:db/id 17592186417188} {:db/id 17592186417189} {:db/id 17592186417191} {:db/id 17592186436249} {:db/id 17592186440463} {:db/id 17592186440467} {:db/id 17592186440468}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in Another Basis"} :step/id #uuid "2c41659c-3fb0-58d9-904f-2296e677eb6c" :step/math-academy-id 26946} {:db/id 17592186125822 :tutorial/content "We've seen that to find the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to a basis $\mathcal B,$ we can use the formula

Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & -8\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-8)-(-3)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-8 & 3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 18\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4de2c56b-39c0-5e14-a7fb-e708db903e6f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436251}} {:db/id 17592186436251 :step/content {:db/id 17592186436248 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "426822c2-147e-581d-8735-96a3bffe8321" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186436236} {:answer/id #uuid "5c39bc95-ae02-5c17-9a57-15db094b94c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186436238} {:answer/id #uuid "89f6cf40-819f-5c6b-aeaf-667b443a0b60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 11\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186436240} {:answer/id #uuid "e55ca324-fff5-5f74-ad7a-3c6af6f7f1cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}36 \\ 13\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186436244} {:answer/id #uuid "ef9b888d-cda8-5e1c-bef9-2a98c4f74288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-22 \\ 27\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186436245}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436238} :answer-field/id #uuid "c1014636-1510-50f6-b488-e3fe8d24c13d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436247}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0e4c9378-b054-5da6-b199-f46a138a46d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-113603" :question/problem "$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 4-6\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4f40a8b0-4293-52f4-8c95-85c75998d506" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436252}} {:db/id 17592186436252 :step/content {:db/id 17592186247379 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05662116-9ed5-51f3-a508-b1ed64f2e349" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186244359} {:answer/id #uuid "33a9596f-e4e0-5e92-b079-84b8cbdda157" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -11\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186244776} {:answer/id #uuid "7294001d-9a70-5e64-8833-bfc2b3f3c0db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}25 \\ 6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186245337} {:answer/id #uuid "b6b79f00-6365-55a2-9673-e57f0f1960c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 21\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186245947} {:answer/id #uuid "f5b08e24-4041-566d-9201-1f4cbd15de31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}19 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186246483}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186244359} :answer-field/id #uuid "12b31fac-75a2-50ec-9978-bbb512fe8ff1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186246582}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "162a4f62-2177-5623-998d-5746dbddde07" :question/math-academy-id "q-113606" :question/problem "$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 6-(-7)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$

$$

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 6-(-7)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f5e3b29d-0add-527d-a99b-25156b6317ea"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e412cca-3de6-5980-bb99-cf3bccf43fec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163117 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion $p$ of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate $A.$"

If the company has $N = 50$ employees, and $30$ of them will vote for candidate $A,$ then the proportion $p$ is given by

$$
p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6.
$$

In other words, $60\%$ of the company's employees will vote for candidate $A.$

Note the following:

- $N$ is the **population size**

- $p$ is the **population proportion**

- The number of employees that will vote for candidate $A$ is given by

$$
Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30.
$$

In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating $p$ in cases where the population size $N$ is very large. Note that although the population size $N$ is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas.

We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable $X_i,$ defined by

![](images/76/76b2ae3dd8206bfdbe208d0e037bd1efa5614101917cf6f981df078cb3cdc8cf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ 

Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate $A$ is straightforward:

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{i}=1) & =\frac{\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A}{\text{population size}} \\  & =\frac{Np}{N} \\  & =\frac{30}{50} \\  & =0.6\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** It's important to note that the $X_i$'s are *dependent!* For example,

$$
P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ).
$$

To see why, note that $P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,$ as before. However,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{(\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A)-1}{\text{population size}-1} \\  & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\  & =\frac{50\cdot 0.6-1}{50-1} \\  & =\frac{30-1}{49} \\  & =\frac{29}{49} \\  & ≈0.592 \\  & \ne P({X}_{2}=1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate $A.$ So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will *also* vote for candidate $A,$ we consider a reduced population with $N-1 = 49$ members, of which only $30-1 = 29$ will vote for candidate $A.$

Calculating $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)$ works similarly, as we'll see in the following example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3fb9dab1-fabb-573d-8f7b-d06c37474163" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6461 :tutorial/title "Properties of Sums of Bernoulli Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "0c4a9d24-fd2f-52ed-94cd-513aa0657bab" :step/math-academy-id 39031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163126}} {:db/id 17592186163124 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163345 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/32/32bc52b6268f6c5eeb9a6f07fff58c308871cc650541c16a4c595faf81e833df.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

It can be shown that the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables *provided that* the population size $N$ is *significantly larger* than the sample size $n$ (which we denote as $N \gg n$). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than $5\%$ of the population size.

The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters. 

Let's now consider the following statistic:

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i
$$

where $X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ 

Since the $X_i$'s take the value $1$ if the $i$th element has the characteristic or $0$ if the $i$th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic $X$ can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic.

We wish to determine the sampling distribution of $X.$ Note the following:

- Each $X_i$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., $X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$

- Since we're assuming that $N\gg n,$ it follows that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are (approximately) *independent and identically distributed* (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables.

- It can be shown that a sum of $n$ I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p$ is a binomial random variable $B(n,p)$ (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

We summarize this process using the following flow chart.

![](images/f5/f50d54432c86d4b41ed842218a70b93617457de3e518aa88cbe6ea28762f37ea.png)

Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77f66879-2dda-57f9-b96c-2ad1166282c8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6477 :tutorial/title "The Number of Sample Elements With a Characteristic"} :step/id #uuid "7f0864d1-c890-56d0-ad56-9af735a0fb71" :step/math-academy-id 39212 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163120}} {:db/id 17592186163125 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163346 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population of size $N=1\,000$ of which the proportion $p=0.5$ has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/a8/a801fdb0d37e38011713448593b185b440445d6a57b0ff42e00c21e66401f6bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.$

Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the $X_i$'s are *dependent*.

This time, however, since the population size $N = 1\,000$ is large, we may *approximate* that the $X_i$'s are *independent*. 

To see why, we first note that 

$$
P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5.
$$

Now, computing $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\  & =\frac{1\,000\cdot 0.5-1}{1\,000-1} \\  & =\frac{500-1}{999} \\  & =\frac{499}{999} \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we've shown that

$$
P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1),
$$

suggesting that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are (approximately) independent." :tutorial/id #uuid "a129ef6b-606a-5b23-8f65-0573d4422fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6479 :tutorial/title "Independence in Large Populations"} :step/id #uuid "16f70a0f-60a9-55ce-a435-a9dd8530d4d9" :step/math-academy-id 39214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163124}} {:db/id 17592186163126 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163347 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows:

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i =  \overline{X}
$$

Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

 

Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\  & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\  & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we have the following important results:

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}
$$

It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8ecb0abb-cc8a-58b3-b310-fabeeb9c4aca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6480 :tutorial/title "Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions"} :step/id #uuid "656c4a52-6bb0-59f8-878d-58db462b17ee" :step/math-academy-id 39215 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163128}} {:db/id 17592186163128 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163349 :tutorial/content "The standard deviation of $\widehat{\,p}$  is called the **standard error** of $\widehat{\,p}$ and is denoted $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}
$$

If $p$ is unknown, we can replace it with its estimate $\widehat{\,p}$ in the standard error formula, as follows:

$$
\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]  = \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}
$$

Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an estimate of $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .$" :tutorial/id #uuid "34af16d9-40e0-5de6-9e2d-753be4cea679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6484 :tutorial/title "The Standard Error"} :step/id #uuid "8e2f6423-528f-586d-8112-c73e1f771a8a" :step/math-academy-id 39234 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163118}}] :activity/title "Sampling Proportions From Finite Populations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162231} {:db/id 17592186163117 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. Calculating $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)$ works similarly, as we'll see in the following example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3fb9dab1-fabb-573d-8f7b-d06c37474163" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6461 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186163119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162138 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161704 :question/id #uuid "b162ec77-b73f-50f7-b2d2-b6c82bdb7d67" :question/math-academy-id "e-10363"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b9274c87-2d68-5fca-af3e-5c47b9541bac" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048456}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162425} {:db/id 17592186162434} {:db/id 17592186441112} {:db/id 17592186441120} {:db/id 17592186441122} {:db/id 17592186441123}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Conditional Probability Given a Population Proportion"} :step/id #uuid "1a5db991-df51-5d92-b1cc-245ea8960755" :step/math-academy-id 39030 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163125}} {:db/id 17592186163118 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162137 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161703 :question/id #uuid "1ad81fed-5e71-5df6-abc4-a09cd5c432fc" :question/math-academy-id "e-10362"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1c6e806b-288e-5ff8-b54d-4b19c16cd2f7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048731} {:db/id 17592186050606}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162431} {:db/id 17592186162439} {:db/id 17592186441113} {:db/id 17592186441114} {:db/id 17592186441115} {:db/id 17592186441116}] :knowledge-point/title "Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions"} :step/id #uuid "3959ad96-797b-5cb6-937c-25ee4bd8fbf5" :step/math-academy-id 39025} {:db/id 17592186163125 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163346 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population of size $N=1\,000$ of which the proportion $p=0.5$ has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/a8/a801fdb0d37e38011713448593b185b440445d6a57b0ff42e00c21e66401f6bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.$

Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the $X_i$'s are *dependent*.

This time, however, since the population size $N = 1\,000$ is large, we may *approximate* that the $X_i$'s are *independent*. 

To see why, we first note that 

$$
P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5.
$$

Now, computing $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\  & =\frac{1\,000\cdot 0.5-1}{1\,000-1} \\  & =\frac{500-1}{999} \\  & =\frac{499}{999} \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we've shown that

$$
P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1),
$$

suggesting that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are (approximately) independent." :tutorial/id #uuid "a129ef6b-606a-5b23-8f65-0573d4422fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6479 :tutorial/title "Independence in Large Populations"} :step/id #uuid "16f70a0f-60a9-55ce-a435-a9dd8530d4d9" :step/math-academy-id 39214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163124}} {:db/id 17592186163120 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162139 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161705 :question/id #uuid "a623014c-203f-5c40-87b5-e847782a8ea1" :question/math-academy-id "e-10364"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e7e5587a-5a45-59b6-ae59-df68ed33e0fb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050425} {:db/id 17592186051082}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162432} {:db/id 17592186162433} {:db/id 17592186441117} {:db/id 17592186441118} {:db/id 17592186441119} {:db/id 17592186441121}] :knowledge-point/title "Properties of Sums of Bernoulli Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "0c4a9d24-fd2f-52ed-94cd-513aa0657bab" :step/math-academy-id 39031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163126}} {:db/id 17592186163126 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163347 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows:

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i =  \overline{X}
$$

Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

 

Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\  & =p.\end{aligned}
$$

For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\  & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we have the following important results:

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}
$$

It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8ecb0abb-cc8a-58b3-b310-fabeeb9c4aca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6480 :tutorial/title "Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions"} :step/id #uuid "656c4a52-6bb0-59f8-878d-58db462b17ee" :step/math-academy-id 39215 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163128}} {:db/id 17592186163124 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163345 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/32/32bc52b6268f6c5eeb9a6f07fff58c308871cc650541c16a4c595faf81e833df.svg)
for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ 

It can be shown that the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables *provided that* the population size $N$ is *significantly larger* than the sample size $n$ (which we denote as $N \gg n$). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than $5\%$ of the population size.

The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters. 

Let's now consider the following statistic:

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i
$$

where $X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ 

Since the $X_i$'s take the value $1$ if the $i$th element has the characteristic or $0$ if the $i$th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic $X$ can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic.

We wish to determine the sampling distribution of $X.$ Note the following:

- Each $X_i$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., $X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$

- Since we're assuming that $N\gg n,$ it follows that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are (approximately) *independent and identically distributed* (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables.

- It can be shown that a sum of $n$ I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p$ is a binomial random variable $B(n,p)$ (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore,

$$
X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).
$$

We summarize this process using the following flow chart.

![](images/f5/f50d54432c86d4b41ed842218a70b93617457de3e518aa88cbe6ea28762f37ea.png)

Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77f66879-2dda-57f9-b96c-2ad1166282c8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6477 :tutorial/title "The Number of Sample Elements With a Characteristic"} :step/id #uuid "7f0864d1-c890-56d0-ad56-9af735a0fb71" :step/math-academy-id 39212 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163120}} {:db/id 17592186163345 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. $$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}

$$

Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an estimate of $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .$" :tutorial/id #uuid "34af16d9-40e0-5de6-9e2d-753be4cea679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6484 :tutorial/title "The Standard Error"} :step/id #uuid "8e2f6423-528f-586d-8112-c73e1f771a8a" :step/math-academy-id 39234 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163118}} {:db/id 17592186163349 :tutorial/content "The standard deviation of $\widehat{\,p}$  is called the **standard error** of $\widehat{\,p}$ and is denoted $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}$

Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an estimate of $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .$" :tutorial/id #uuid "34af16d9-40e0-5de6-9e2d-753be4cea679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6484 :tutorial/title "The Standard Error"} {:db/id 17592186054654 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054384 :question/id #uuid "8955a3ce-a161-5dc5-8ec0-c357a0403b46" :question/math-academy-id "e-12862"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b170bf27-76bc-5558-9133-e81a4760072f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048725} {:db/id 17592186050613}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186054941 :question/id #uuid "ffe64c93-a4c0-5c06-adca-de63e31673ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-101792"} {:db/id 17592186055056 :question/id #uuid "e2c6fc89-ff49-59a4-9fee-dedf51fc71ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-175698"} {:db/id 17592186055227 :question/id #uuid "e779cd48-6b59-57a9-9d72-5b6202314909" :question/math-academy-id "q-319"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations that Involve Multiplication"} {:db/id 17592186054384 :question/id #uuid "8955a3ce-a161-5dc5-8ec0-c357a0403b46" :question/math-academy-id "e-12862" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054654 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b170bf27-76bc-5558-9133-e81a4760072f" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations that Involve Multiplication"}] :question/problem "Solve the equation $3p-7 =20$." :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, adding $7$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned} 3p-7 &=20 \\ 3p-7+7 &=20+7 \\ 3p + 0 &= 27 \\ 3p &=27 \end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 3p &=27 \\[5pt] \dfrac{3p}{3} &=\dfrac{27}{3} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\cancel{3}p}{\cancel{3}} &= 9 \\[5pt] p &=9 \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050613} {:db/id 17592186054941 :question/id #uuid "ffe64c93-a4c0-5c06-adca-de63e31673ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-101792"} {:db/id 17592186055056 :question/id #uuid "e2c6fc89-ff49-59a4-9fee-dedf51fc71ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-175698"} {:db/id 17592186055227 :question/id #uuid "e779cd48-6b59-57a9-9d72-5b6202314909" :question/math-academy-id "q-319"} {:db/id 17592186054655 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054385 :question/id #uuid "074b5213-4f4e-5d1b-a5c4-8b5403901b4d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12863"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "52c2b31a-9b7a-52cb-9fa7-111de8bc53ea" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055057 :question/id #uuid "9ac43319-fc4a-5b3e-be95-327e9d71adda" :question/math-academy-id "q-175702"} {:db/id 17592186055058 :question/id #uuid "9b7a4ee1-37bd-5a89-b3b0-0207e92de656" :question/math-academy-id "q-175707"} {:db/id 17592186055059 :question/id #uuid "2497f38a-0c5a-5632-a4d5-cd45c561a2fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-175708"} {:db/id 17592186055279 :question/id #uuid "bb9596d7-9c40-5940-99ee-4fc5700e6eea" :question/math-academy-id "q-43948"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations while Keeping the Variable on the Right-Hand Side"} {:db/id 17592186054385 :question/id #uuid "074b5213-4f4e-5d1b-a5c4-8b5403901b4d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12863" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054655 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "52c2b31a-9b7a-52cb-9fa7-111de8bc53ea" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations while Keeping the Variable on the Right-Hand Side"}] :question/problem "Solve for $x$ where $2=5x-8$." :question/worked-solution "To save time, we will keep the variable on the right-hand side as we solve. First, we apply the addition principle, adding $8$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 &= 5x - 8 \\
2 + 8 &= 5x - 8 + 8 \\
10 &= 5x + 0 \\
10 &= 5x
\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $5$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
10 &= 5x \\
\frac{10}{5} &= \frac{5x}{5} \\
2 &= \frac{5x}{5} \\
2 &= x
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2=x$, we conclude that the solution is $x=2$."} {:db/id 17592186055057 :question/id #uuid "9ac43319-fc4a-5b3e-be95-327e9d71adda" :question/math-academy-id "q-175702"} {:db/id 17592186055058 :question/id #uuid "9b7a4ee1-37bd-5a89-b3b0-0207e92de656" :question/math-academy-id "q-175707"} {:db/id 17592186055059 :question/id #uuid "2497f38a-0c5a-5632-a4d5-cd45c561a2fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-175708"} {:db/id 17592186055279 :question/id #uuid "bb9596d7-9c40-5940-99ee-4fc5700e6eea" :question/math-academy-id "q-43948"} {:db/id 17592186054656 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054386 :question/id #uuid "1f5b9030-a5de-5ac2-95c4-2fbaf638cdab" :question/math-academy-id "e-12864"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ac53e171-0a02-5b74-8a3a-465dbecda9d7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055178 :question/id #uuid "b0f90932-2e60-5294-a78f-433c00be41b1" :question/math-academy-id "q-2535"} {:db/id 17592186055273 :question/id #uuid "90f89fec-4a6a-5809-8911-0d6643c1e229" :question/math-academy-id "q-427"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations that Involve Division"} {:db/id 17592186054386 :question/id #uuid "1f5b9030-a5de-5ac2-95c4-2fbaf638cdab" :question/math-academy-id "e-12864" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054656 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ac53e171-0a02-5b74-8a3a-465dbecda9d7" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Linear Equations that Involve Division"}] :question/problem "Solve the equation $7-\dfrac{p}{3} =9$." :question/worked-solution "After converting the equation to a more familiar form, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $7$ from both sides:

$$
\require{cancel} \begin{aligned} 7-\dfrac{p}{3} &=9 \\ -\dfrac{p}{3}+7 &=9 \\ -\dfrac{p}{3}+7-7 &= 9-7 \\ -\dfrac{p}{3}+0 &= 2 \\ -\dfrac{p}{3} &=2 \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle. We multiply by $-1$ to get rid of the negative sign, and again by $3$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
